notes:
1. Bahmani Kingdom — Overview

  • The Bahmani Kingdom was the first major independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan.
  • It was founded in 1347 CE.
  • It emerged when the authority of the Delhi Sultanate weakened in the Deccan.
  • For nearly two centuries, it remained one of the most important political powers of peninsular India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahmani Kingdom → 1347 CE

2. Founder

  • The Bahmani Kingdom was founded by Ala-ud-Din Hasan Bahman Shah.
  • Before assuming kingship, he was known as Hasan Gangu in several historical traditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Founder → Ala-ud-Din Hasan Bahman Shah

3. Hasan Gangu

  • Hasan Bahman Shah is frequently referred to in historical accounts as Hasan Gangu.
  • The exact origin of the name "Gangu" and stories connecting him with a Brahmana patron are uncertain and partly legendary.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Hasan Gangu Tradition → Commonly Mentioned, But Details of Early Life Are Uncertain

4. Background — Muhammad bin Tughlaq

  • The Bahmani state emerged during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
  • Rebellions in the Deccan weakened Delhi's control.
  • Deccan nobles established an independent kingdom in 1347.

5. Independence from Delhi Sultanate

  • The foundation of the Bahmani Kingdom represented the permanent weakening of direct Delhi Sultanate control over much of the Deccan.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bahmani Rise → Decline of Tughlaq Authority in Deccan

6. First Capital

  • The first capital of the Bahmani Kingdom was Gulbarga.
  • Hasan Bahman Shah renamed it Ahsanabad.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Bahmani Capital → Gulbarga / Ahsanabad

7. Gulbarga

  • Gulbarga is in present-day Karnataka.
  • It became the political and military centre of the early Bahmani state.

8. Second Capital

  • The capital was later shifted from Gulbarga to Bidar.
  • Ahmad Shah I Wali is associated with this transfer during the fifteenth century.
📌 Must-Memorise

Later Bahmani Capital → Bidar

9. Gulbarga to Bidar

  • Memory:
  • Gulbarga → Early Bahmani
  • Bidar → Later Bahmani

10. Geographical Extent

  • At different times Bahmani authority covered large parts of:
  • Northern Karnataka.
  • Telangana.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Parts of Andhra region.

11. Bahmani–Vijayanagara Rivalry

  • The Bahmani Kingdom and Vijayanagara Empire were major rivals.
  • Their conflicts lasted for generations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahmani's Major Southern Rival → Vijayanagara

12. Raichur Doab

  • The Raichur Doab was the most famous disputed region between the two powers.
  • It lies between:
  • Krishna River.
  • Tungabhadra River.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raichur Doab → Krishna + Tungabhadra

13. Why Raichur Was Important

  • The Raichur Doab was valuable because of:
  • Fertile black soil.
  • Agricultural revenue.
  • Strategic forts.
  • Routes linking northern and southern Deccan.

14. Krishna–Tungabhadra Frontier

  • The river zone between Krishna and Tungabhadra became a recurring military frontier.
  • Raichur and Mudgal were particularly important forts.

15. Mudgal Fort

  • Mudgal was a strategic fort in the Raichur region.
  • It changed hands during Bahmani–Vijayanagara conflicts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mudgal + Raichur → Bahmani–Vijayanagara Conflict Zone

16. Hasan Bahman Shah

  • Hasan Bahman Shah ruled from 1347 to 1358.
  • He consolidated the new Sultanate.
  • Gulbarga was his capital.

17. Hasan Bahman Shah's Expansion

  • His authority extended across important parts of the northern Deccan through:
  • Military campaigns.
  • Submission of local chiefs.
  • Reorganisation of provinces.

18. Administrative Divisions

  • The early Bahmani state was divided into large provinces called Tarafs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahmani Province → Taraf

19. Tarafdar

  • The governor of a Taraf was called a Tarafdar.
  • Tarafdars exercised:
  • Military.
  • Revenue.
  • Administrative powers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Taraf → Tarafdar

20. Muhammad Shah I

  • Muhammad Shah I succeeded Hasan Bahman Shah.
  • He ruled from 1358 to 1375.
  • His reign saw major wars with Vijayanagara and Warangal.

21. Warangal

  • Warangal was an important political centre in Telangana.
  • Bahmani rulers repeatedly competed for control over Telangana territories and forts.

22. Bahmani–Warangal Relations

  • Relations involved:
  • Warfare.
  • Tribute.
  • Territorial transfers.
  • Strategic alliances.

23. Muhammad Shah I and Vijayanagara

  • Conflict with Vijayanagara intensified over the Raichur Doab.
  • The wars demonstrated the military importance of cavalry, forts and artillery.

24. Early Gunpowder Warfare

  • The Deccan witnessed increasing use of gunpowder weapons during the late medieval period.
  • Bahmani and Vijayanagara armies gradually incorporated artillery.

25. Mujahid Shah

  • Mujahid Shah succeeded Muhammad Shah I.
  • He continued military operations against Vijayanagara.
  • His reign was short.

26. Muhammad Shah II

  • Muhammad Shah II ruled during the late fourteenth century.
  • His reign is generally remembered as comparatively peaceful.
  • Cultural and educational activities received patronage.

27. Firuz Shah Bahmani

  • Taj-ud-Din Firuz Shah became one of the most notable Bahmani rulers.
  • He ruled from 1397 to 1422.
📌 Must-Memorise

Firuz Shah Bahmani → 1397–1422

28. Firuz Shah — Scholar

  • Firuz Shah was known for intellectual interests.
  • Chronicles describe him as knowledgeable in:
  • Languages.
  • Theology.
  • Literature.
  • Science.

29. Firuz Shah and Vijayanagara

  • Firuz Shah fought several campaigns against Vijayanagara.
  • The Raichur region remained central to these conflicts.

30. Marriage Alliance

  • After one of his campaigns against Vijayanagara, Firuz Shah entered a matrimonial alliance involving the Vijayanagara royal family according to medieval chronicles.
  • Details vary across historical sources.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Bahmani–Vijayanagara Relations → Warfare Plus Occasional Diplomacy

31. Pangul / Panagal Campaign

  • Firuz Shah suffered an important military setback in the Telangana-Andhra region toward the end of his reign.
  • This weakened his political position.

32. Ahmad Shah I

  • Ahmad Shah I succeeded Firuz Shah in 1422.
  • He is popularly known as Ahmad Shah Wali.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ahmad Shah I → Ahmad Shah Wali

33. Ahmad Shah Wali

  • Ahmad Shah was associated with Sufi traditions.
  • His tomb at Ashtur near Bidar became an important devotional site.

34. Capital Shift to Bidar

  • Ahmad Shah I shifted the Bahmani political centre from Gulbarga to Bidar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Capital Shift → Ahmad Shah I → Bidar

35. Why Bidar Was Chosen

  • Bidar offered:
  • Strong defensive position.
  • Better access to eastern Deccan.
  • Strategic location.
  • Favourable climate compared with some surrounding plains.

36. Bidar Fort

  • Bidar Fort became a major royal and military complex.
  • It was expanded and modified under Bahmani and later Barid Shahi rulers.

37. Ahmad Shah and Warangal

  • Bahmani forces expanded deeper into Telangana under Ahmad Shah.
  • Warangal's political independence was severely weakened.

38. Bahmani Expansion in Telangana

  • Control over Telangana provided:
  • Agricultural revenue.
  • Strategic forts.
  • Routes toward eastern coastal areas.

39. Ala-ud-Din Ahmad II

  • Ala-ud-Din Ahmad II succeeded Ahmad Shah I.
  • His reign continued Bahmani involvement in Deccan warfare and court factionalism.

40. Humayun Shah

  • Humayun Shah ruled briefly in the mid-fifteenth century.
  • His reign was marked by political instability.

41. Nizam Shah

  • Nizam Shah succeeded Humayun as a minor.
  • Powerful ministers and nobles exercised major influence during his short reign.

42. Muhammad Shah III

  • Muhammad Shah III became Sultan while young.
  • His reign is especially important because of his minister Mahmud Gawan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahmud Gawan → Muhammad Shah III Period

43. Mahmud Gawan

  • Mahmud Gawan was the greatest minister of the Bahmani Kingdom.
  • He was originally from Persia.
  • He became:
  • Merchant.
  • Scholar.
  • Statesman.
  • Military commander.
📌 Must-Memorise

Great Bahmani Minister → Mahmud Gawan

44. Origin of Mahmud Gawan

  • Mahmud Gawan came from the Persian world.
  • He arrived in the Deccan during the fifteenth century.
  • He belonged to the group of foreign-born nobles generally called Afaqis.

45. Afaqi

  • Afaqis were nobles who had come to the Deccan from overseas regions, especially:
  • Persia.
  • Central Asia.
  • Arab regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Afaqi → Foreign/Overseas Nobles

46. Deccani Nobles

  • Deccanis were older-established Muslim elites of the Deccan.
  • They included locally rooted Muslim groups and earlier immigrants whose families had settled in the region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deccani → Established Local Deccan Muslim Elite

47. Deccani–Afaqi Conflict

  • Rivalry between Deccani and Afaqi nobles became one of the most serious internal problems of the Bahmani state.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bahmani Internal Conflict → Deccani vs Afaqi

48. Causes of Factional Conflict

  • Conflict developed over:
  • Government posts.
  • Land assignments.
  • Military commands.
  • Royal influence.
  • Cultural and regional identity.

49. Mahmud Gawan as Wazir

  • Mahmud Gawan became the leading minister or Wazir.
  • He attempted to strengthen the Sultan's authority over powerful provincial nobles.

50. Mahmud Gawan's Military Achievements

  • His campaigns expanded Bahmani influence in:
  • Konkan.
  • Western coast.
  • Eastern Deccan.

51. Goa

  • Bahmani forces gained control of Goa for a period during Mahmud Gawan's military campaigns.
  • Goa was important for maritime commerce and horse imports.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mahmud Gawan → Western Coastal Expansion

52. Importance of Western Coast

  • Western ports provided access to:
  • Arabian horse trade.
  • Persian Gulf commerce.
  • Customs revenue.
  • Imported luxury goods.

53. Mahmud Gawan's Administrative Reforms

  • His reforms aimed to:
  • Reduce provincial governors' power.
  • Strengthen central government.
  • Improve revenue assessment.
  • Maintain a disciplined army.

54. Reorganisation of Tarafs

  • The Bahmani kingdom had earlier been divided into fewer large Tarafs.
  • Mahmud Gawan reorganised the state into eight Tarafs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahmud Gawan → Eight Tarafs

55. Reason for Eight Tarafs

  • Smaller provinces reduced the possibility of extremely powerful governors challenging the Sultan.

56. Khalsa Land

  • Mahmud Gawan increased the amount of land under direct royal control.
  • Such crown-controlled territory provided revenue directly to the central treasury.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mahmud Gawan → Stronger Khalsa / Crown Lands

57. Land Measurement

  • Mahmud Gawan promoted systematic measurement of cultivated land.
  • Revenue demand was linked more closely to land and productivity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahmud Gawan → Land Measurement Reform

58. Control of Tarafdars

  • Tarafdars were required to maintain forces according to their assignments.
  • Central supervision sought to prevent misuse of revenue.

59. Fort Control

  • Mahmud Gawan limited the number of forts directly controlled by provincial governors.
  • Important forts were placed under officers appointed by the Sultan.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gawan → Reduced Tarafdar Military Independence

60. Salaries

  • Officials could receive cash salaries or revenue assignments.
  • Gawan attempted to connect income more carefully with official responsibilities.

61. Mahmud Gawan Madrasa

  • Mahmud Gawan founded a famous madrasa at Bidar.
  • It became an important centre of higher learning.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahmud Gawan Madrasa → Bidar

62. Madrasa Architecture

  • The madrasa displayed strong Persian architectural influence through:
  • Tall façades.
  • Minarets.
  • Coloured tile decoration.
  • Large courtyard.

63. Subjects at the Madrasa

  • Learning included:
  • Theology.
  • Law.
  • Mathematics.
  • Astronomy.
  • Literature.

64. Library

  • The Mahmud Gawan Madrasa possessed an important library.
  • It reflected the minister's reputation as a scholar.

65. Execution of Mahmud Gawan

  • Rival nobles conspired against Mahmud Gawan.
  • A forged letter was used to accuse him of treason.
  • Muhammad Shah III ordered his execution in 1481.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahmud Gawan Executed → 1481

66. Consequence of Gawan's Death

  • His execution:
  • Weakened central administration.
  • Intensified factional conflict.
  • Strengthened provincial nobles.
  • Accelerated Bahmani decline.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Death of Mahmud Gawan → Major Turning Point in Bahmani Decline

67. Muhammad Shah III's Later Years

  • The Sultan reportedly regretted Gawan's execution.
  • The political damage, however, could not be reversed.

68. Mahmud Shah Bahmani II

  • Mahmud Shah Bahmani II became Sultan during the final phase of the dynasty.
  • Provincial governors became increasingly independent during his long reign.

69. Weakening Central Authority

  • By the late fifteenth century:
  • Sultan's authority declined.
  • Ministers and governors became autonomous.
  • Factional rivalry intensified.

70. Bahmani Disintegration

  • The Bahmani Kingdom fragmented gradually from the late fifteenth century.
  • Five major successor Sultanates emerged.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahmani Breakup → Five Deccan Sultanates

71. Five Deccan Sultanates

  • They were:
  • Ahmadnagar → Nizam Shahi.
  • Bijapur → Adil Shahi.
  • Berar → Imad Shahi.
  • Bidar → Barid Shahi.
  • Golconda → Qutb Shahi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ahmadnagar – Nizam

Bijapur – Adil

Berar – Imad

Bidar – Barid

Golconda – Qutb

72. Ahmadnagar Sultanate

  • Ahmadnagar was founded by Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah.
  • It became known as the Nizam Shahi Sultanate.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ahmadnagar → Nizam Shahi

73. Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah

  • Malik Ahmad established independent authority in the western Deccan around 1490.
  • Ahmadnagar became his capital.

74. Bijapur Sultanate

  • Bijapur was ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty.
  • Yusuf Adil Shah established its independent power.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bijapur → Adil Shahi → Yusuf Adil Shah

75. Berar Sultanate

  • Berar became independent under Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk.
  • Its dynasty was called Imad Shahi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Berar → Imad Shahi

76. Bidar Sultanate

  • Bidar came under the Barid Shahi dynasty.
  • Qasim Barid established the family's political dominance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bidar → Barid Shahi

77. Golconda Sultanate

  • Golconda became independent under the Qutb Shahi dynasty.
  • Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk established autonomous rule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Golconda → Qutb Shahi

78. Bahmani Sultanate's Formal End

  • Even after real power fragmented, nominal Bahmani Sultans survived for some time.
  • By the early sixteenth century, effective imperial authority had disappeared.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bahmani Breakup → Gradual, Not a Single-Year Sudden Collapse

79. Five Sultanates — Geographic Memory

  • Ahmadnagar → Western Maharashtra.
  • Bijapur → Northern Karnataka.
  • Berar → Vidarbha.
  • Bidar → Northern Karnataka.
  • Golconda → Telangana.

80. Deccan Sultanates and Vijayanagara

  • The successor Sultanates frequently fought one another.
  • They also formed temporary alliances against Vijayanagara.

81. Battle of Talikota

  • In 1565, major Deccan Sultanates formed a coalition against Vijayanagara.
  • Vijayanagara was defeated at the Battle of Talikota.
📌 Must-Memorise

1565 → Talikota → Deccan Sultanates Defeated Vijayanagara

82. Bahmani vs Talikota — Trap

  • The original Bahmani Kingdom did not itself fight the Battle of Talikota as a unified state.
  • Its successor Sultanates fought Vijayanagara.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Talikota → Bahmani Successor States, Not Unified Bahmani Kingdom

83. Principal Talikota Allies

  • The principal coalition included:
  • Ahmadnagar.
  • Bijapur.
  • Golconda.
  • Bidar.
  • Berar is generally not listed as a principal participant.

84. Bahmani Administration — Sultan

  • The Sultan was the supreme political and military authority.
  • He appointed:
  • Ministers.
  • Provincial governors.
  • Military officers.
  • Judges.

85. Wazir

  • The Wazir was the chief minister.
  • He coordinated central administration.

86. Wakil-us-Saltana

  • Wakil-us-Saltana was a very high-ranking official who could act as deputy of the Sultan.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wakil-us-Saltana → Deputy of Sultan

87. Amir-i-Jumla

  • Amir-i-Jumla was associated with financial and administrative responsibilities.
  • Titles and functions could change across reigns.

88. Wazir-i-Ashraf

  • Wazir-i-Ashraf handled important affairs connected with foreign relations and the royal court in some administrative descriptions.

89. Peshwa

  • The title Peshwa was also used in Deccan administration before its later famous association with the Marathas.
  • It referred to a high-ranking minister.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Peshwa Title → Existed Before Maratha Peshwas

90. Kotwal

  • Kotwal was responsible for city:
  • Policing.
  • Law and order.
  • Market supervision.

91. Qazi

  • Qazis administered justice according to Islamic law in relevant cases.

92. Sadr

  • The Sadr supervised religious grants and institutions.

93. Provincial Administration

  • Large provinces were called Tarafs.
  • Powerful Tarafdars often became a threat to central authority.

94. Tarafdar Responsibilities

  • Tarafdars:
  • Collected revenue.
  • Maintained troops.
  • Preserved law and order.
  • Administered provincial territory.

95. Centralisation Problem

  • Large provincial commands gave Tarafdars substantial resources.
  • Mahmud Gawan's reforms were designed partly to reduce this danger.

96. Military Organisation

  • The Bahmani military included:
  • Cavalry.
  • Infantry.
  • Elephants.
  • Artillery.
  • Fort garrisons.

97. Cavalry

  • Cavalry remained one of the most important military arms.
  • High-quality horses were imported through western ports.

98. Horse Imports

  • Horses came from:
  • Arabia.
  • Persia.
  • Central Asian networks.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deccan Cavalry → Dependent on Imported Horses

99. Artillery

  • Bahmani armies increasingly used:
  • Cannons.
  • Gunpowder.
  • Military technology developed further under the successor Sultanates.

100. Forts

  • Important forts included:
  • Gulbarga.
  • Bidar.
  • Raichur.
  • Mudgal.
  • Other Deccan strongholds.

101. Land Revenue

  • Agriculture was the principal source of state income.
  • Land revenue was collected from cultivators and villages.

102. Agricultural Regions

  • Important agricultural areas produced:
  • Jowar.
  • Bajra.
  • Rice.
  • Pulses.
  • Cotton.
  • Sugarcane.

103. Irrigation

  • Agriculture depended on:
  • Tanks.
  • Wells.
  • Rivers.
  • Local channels.

104. Black Soil

  • Parts of the Deccan contain fertile black cotton soil.
  • This supported cotton and other crops.

105. Trade

  • The Bahmani Kingdom participated in:
  • Inland Deccan trade.
  • Arabian Sea commerce.
  • Persian Gulf networks.

106. Major Trading Commodities

  • Exports included:
  • Cotton textiles.
  • Rice.
  • Indigo.
  • Agricultural goods.
  • Imports included:
  • Horses.
  • Luxury goods.
  • Metals.

107. Horse Trade

  • The horse trade was strategically important because cavalry quality directly affected military strength.
  • Persian Gulf merchants played an important role.

108. Ports

  • Bahmani competition for the west coast was driven by access to ports such as those in:
  • Konkan.
  • Goa region.
  • Western Karnataka coast.

109. Goa's Importance

  • Goa offered:
  • Excellent harbour connections.
  • Horse imports.
  • Customs revenue.
  • Access to Arabian Sea commerce.

110. Urban Centres

  • Important Bahmani cities included:
  • Gulbarga.
  • Bidar.
  • Daulatabad.
  • Berar-region centres.
  • Deccan trading towns.

111. Bidar as Cultural Centre

  • Bidar developed into an important centre of:
  • Persian culture.
  • Architecture.
  • Education.
  • Sufi traditions.

112. Persian Influence

  • Persian influence appeared in:
  • Court language.
  • Architecture.
  • Literature.
  • Administration.
  • Migration of scholars and nobles.

113. Court Language

  • Persian was the principal language of high administration and court culture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahmani Court Language → Persian

114. Dakhni / Deccani Language

  • A form of early Urdu known as Dakhni or Deccani developed in the Deccan.
  • It reflected interaction among:
  • Persian.
  • Arabic.
  • Local Indo-Aryan.
  • Dravidian linguistic environments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dakhni → Medieval Deccan Cultural Synthesis

115. Dakhni Literature

  • Dakhni later flourished strongly under the Deccan Sultanates.
  • Its roots were connected with the multicultural society of the Bahmani period.

116. Bahmani Society

  • Society included:
  • Deccani Muslims.
  • Foreign Muslim migrants.
  • Hindus of diverse communities.
  • Merchants.
  • Artisans.
  • Peasants.
  • Military elites.

117. Hindu Officials

  • Hindu administrators and local elites also participated in the political and revenue systems.
  • Bahmani governance depended heavily on established Deccan social structures.

118. Cultural Interaction

  • The Deccan became a zone of interaction among:
  • Persian traditions.
  • Islamic culture.
  • Kannada culture.
  • Telugu culture.
  • Marathi culture.
  • Local religious traditions.

119. Sufism

  • Sufi saints and shrines were influential in the Bahmani Deccan.
  • Gulbarga and Bidar developed important Sufi connections.

120. Khwaja Bande Nawaz Gesu Daraz

  • Gesu Daraz was a famous Chishti Sufi saint.
  • He settled at Gulbarga.
  • His shrine remains one of the most important Sufi centres of the Deccan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gesu Daraz → Gulbarga → Chishti Sufi

121. Gesu Daraz and Delhi

  • Gesu Daraz had earlier been associated with the Chishti tradition of Delhi.
  • He moved to the Deccan during the political disturbances of the late fourteenth century.

122. Gulbarga Dargah

  • The dargah of Gesu Daraz at Gulbarga became a major pilgrimage centre.

123. Ahmad Shah Wali

  • Ahmad Shah I also developed a reputation for spiritual devotion.
  • His tomb complex at Ashtur became associated with popular reverence.

124. Bahmani Architecture

  • Major architectural features included:
  • Domes.
  • Arches.
  • Fortifications.
  • Mosques.
  • Tombs.
  • Persian tile work.
  • Local Deccan construction traditions.

125. Gulbarga Fort

  • Gulbarga Fort was an important military centre of the early Bahmani kingdom.
  • It contains the famous Jama Masjid.

126. Gulbarga Jama Masjid

  • The Jama Masjid at Gulbarga is one of the most distinctive Bahmani monuments.
  • Its design includes:
  • Covered courtyard.
  • Multiple domes.
  • Arched bays.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jama Masjid → Gulbarga → Bahmani Architecture

127. Architectural Distinction

  • Unlike many Indian congregational mosques, the Gulbarga Jama Masjid's courtyard is largely roofed.
  • This makes it architecturally distinctive.

128. Haft Gumbaz

  • Haft Gumbaz is a group of Bahmani royal tombs at Gulbarga.
  • The name means "Seven Domes."
📌 Must-Memorise

Haft Gumbaz → Gulbarga

129. Bidar Fort

  • Bidar Fort contains important Bahmani and later Deccan structures.
  • The capital transfer stimulated extensive construction.

130. Mahmud Gawan Madrasa

  • Key facts:
  • Located at Bidar.
  • Founded by Mahmud Gawan.
  • Persian architectural influence.
  • Educational institution.
  • Famous tile decoration.

131. Ashtur Tombs

  • The royal necropolis at Ashtur near Bidar contains tombs of Bahmani rulers.
  • Ahmad Shah Wali's tomb is especially important.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ashtur → Bahmani Royal Tombs

132. Bidriware

  • Bidar became famous for a distinctive metal craft called Bidriware.
  • It involves silver inlay on a darkened metal surface.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bidriware → Bidar

133. Bidriware Material

  • Traditional Bidriware generally uses a zinc-rich alloy.
  • Silver is inlaid into the darkened surface.

134. Cultural Origin of Bidriware

  • Bidri craft developed through interaction between Persian artistic traditions and local Deccan craftsmanship.

135. Bahmani Art and Architecture

  • The Bahmani artistic tradition contributed to later architectural styles of:
  • Bijapur.
  • Bidar.
  • Golconda.
  • Ahmadnagar.

136. Bahmani–Vijayanagara Cultural Interaction

  • Although politically hostile, the two states shared:
  • Military technologies.
  • Commercial networks.
  • Artisans.
  • Architectural influences.
  • Diplomatic practices.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Political Rivalry ≠ Complete Cultural Isolation

137. Military Recruitment Across Religion

  • Both Bahmani and Vijayanagara rulers employed soldiers from diverse religious and regional backgrounds.
  • Military necessity often crossed religious boundaries.

138. Bahmani–Tamil Nadu Connection

  • The Bahmani Kingdom itself was centred north of the Tamil region.
  • Its Tamil Nadu relevance comes primarily through:
  • Vijayanagara rivalry.
  • Deccan politics.
  • Later successor Sultanates.
  • Battle of Talikota and the consequent strengthening of Tamil Nayak autonomy.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Bahmani Legacy → Deccan Sultanates → Talikota → Rise of Stronger Nayak States in Tamil Region

139. Talikota and Tamil Nadu

  • Vijayanagara's defeat in 1565 weakened imperial control over its southern provinces.
  • Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee Nayaks became increasingly autonomous afterward.

140. Golconda and Coromandel

  • The Qutb Shahi successor state of Golconda later became deeply involved in trade and politics along the Telugu and Coromandel coasts.
  • This indirectly affected northern Tamil coastal politics.

141. Bijapur and South Indian Politics

  • The Adil Shahi state of Bijapur competed with:
  • Vijayanagara.
  • Marathas.
  • Mughals.
  • Its influence shaped the wider political environment of the Deccan.

142. Ahmadnagar and Maratha Rise

  • The Nizam Shahi state of Ahmadnagar later employed many Maratha families.
  • Shahaji Bhonsle served the Ahmadnagar political system during part of his career.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ahmadnagar Nizam Shahi → Important Background to Maratha Rise

143. Deccan Political Continuity

  • Sequence:
  • Bahmani Kingdom
  • → Five Deccan Sultanates
  • → Mughal–Deccan conflict
  • → Maratha expansion
📌 Must-Memorise

Bahmani History → Foundation for Later Deccan Politics

144. Deccan Sultanates and Mughal Empire

  • The successor Sultanates later came under Mughal pressure.
  • Major outcomes:
  • Ahmadnagar gradually absorbed.
  • Bijapur annexed in 1686.
  • Golconda annexed in 1687.

145. Bahmani vs Mughal Chronology

  • Bahmani state began more than a century before Mughal rule in India.
  • Babur founded the Mughal Empire only in 1526.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bahmani 1347 → Earlier Than Mughal 1526

146. Bahmani vs Vijayanagara Chronology

  • Vijayanagara → 1336.
  • Bahmani → 1347.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vijayanagara Older by 11 Years

147. Religious Patronage

  • Bahmani rulers patronised:
  • Mosques.
  • Madrasas.
  • Sufi establishments.
  • Scholars.
  • Local non-Muslim institutions also continued across much of the kingdom.

148. Education

  • Centres of learning were supported at:
  • Gulbarga.
  • Bidar.
  • Madrasas.
  • Sufi centres.

149. Mahmud Gawan as Scholar

  • Mahmud Gawan was known for scholarship in addition to politics.
  • His educational patronage made Bidar an important intellectual centre.

150. Revenue and Army Relationship

  • Provincial revenue financed local military contingents.
  • This made Tarafdars powerful.
  • Gawan's reforms attempted to ensure that provincial resources served central authority.

151. Bahmani Political Weakness

  • The major structural problem was:
  • Powerful Provinces + Factional Nobility + Weak Sultans

152. Role of Young Sultans

  • Several later Bahmani rulers came to the throne at a young age.
  • This increased the influence of:
  • Regents.
  • Ministers.
  • Court factions.

153. Provincial Autonomy

  • As central control weakened, governors began:
  • Keeping more revenue.
  • Maintaining independent armies.
  • Forming regional dynasties.

154. Reasons for Bahmani Decline

  • Important factors included:
  • Deccani–Afaqi conflict.
  • Weak later rulers.
  • Powerful provincial governors.
  • Court conspiracies.
  • Execution of Mahmud Gawan.
  • Continuous warfare.
  • Succession disputes.

155. Mahmud Gawan and Decline

  • Gawan was perhaps the last major administrator capable of preserving strong central authority.
  • His execution removed an important stabilising force.

156. Five Sultanates — Dynasty Memory

  • Nizam → Ahmadnagar.
  • Adil → Bijapur.
  • Imad → Berar.
  • Barid → Bidar.
  • Qutb → Golconda.

157. Capital Memory

  • Bahmani:
  • Gulbarga → First.
  • Bidar → Later.
  • Successor Sultanates:
  • Ahmadnagar → Nizam Shahi.
  • Bijapur → Adil Shahi.
  • Bidar → Barid Shahi.
  • Golconda → Qutb Shahi.

158. Major Person–Place Pairings

  • Hasan Bahman Shah → Gulbarga.
  • Ahmad Shah Wali → Bidar.
  • Mahmud Gawan → Bidar.
  • Gesu Daraz → Gulbarga.
  • Raichur → Krishna–Tungabhadra Doab.

159. Person–Contribution Pairings

  • Hasan Bahman Shah → Founder.
  • Ahmad Shah Wali → Capital to Bidar.
  • Firuz Shah → Major scholar-ruler.
  • Mahmud Gawan → Administrative reform.
  • Muhammad Shah III → Gawan's Sultan.
  • Qasim Barid → Bidar successor state.
  • Yusuf Adil Shah → Bijapur.
  • Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah → Ahmadnagar.
  • Sultan Quli → Golconda.

160. Mahmud Gawan — Quick Facts

  • Persian origin.
  • Afaqi noble.
  • Great Wazir.
  • Eight Tarafs.
  • Land measurement.
  • Reduced provincial power.
  • Strengthened crown lands.
  • Built Madrasa at Bidar.
  • Executed in 1481.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahmud Gawan → Administration + Madrasa + 1481

161. Bahmani Architecture — Quick Facts

  • Gulbarga Jama Masjid.
  • Haft Gumbaz.
  • Bidar Fort.
  • Ashtur tombs.
  • Mahmud Gawan Madrasa.

162. Bahmani Cultural Quick Facts

  • Persian court culture.
  • Dakhni linguistic development.
  • Sufi influence.
  • Bidri metal craft.
  • Persian-local architectural synthesis.

163. Bahmani Economic Quick Facts

  • Agriculture → Base.
  • Horse imports → Military importance.
  • West-coast ports → Maritime trade.
  • Cotton → Important crop and commodity.
  • Customs → Revenue source.

164. Bahmani Military Quick Facts

  • Cavalry.
  • Infantry.
  • Elephants.
  • Artillery.
  • Forts.
  • Imported horses.

165. Bahmani–Vijayanagara Quick Comparison

  • Vijayanagara:
  • Founded 1336.
  • Capital Hampi.
  • Sangama first dynasty.
  • Bahmani:
  • Founded 1347.
  • Capital first Gulbarga.
  • Later Bidar.
  • Shared conflict:
  • Raichur Doab.

166. Raichur Doab — Common Trap

  • Krishna is the northern river.
  • Tungabhadra lies to the south.
  • The land between them is the Raichur Doab.

167. Bahmani and Warangal

  • Warangal/Telangana formed another major eastern zone of competition.
  • Bahmani expansion gradually weakened independent Telangana powers.

168. Bahmani and Konkan

  • Control of the Konkan meant access to:
  • Ports.
  • Horse imports.
  • Customs.
  • Mahmud Gawan's western campaigns were therefore strategically important.

169. Bahmani Legacy

  • The Bahmani Kingdom left a major legacy in:
  • Deccan administration.
  • Architecture.
  • Dakhni culture.
  • Sufi traditions.
  • Military organisation.
  • Formation of five Sultanates.

170. Deccan Cultural Synthesis

  • The Bahmani period contributed to a distinctive Deccan culture combining:
  • Persian.
  • Turkish.
  • Arabic.
  • Marathi.
  • Kannada.
  • Telugu influences.

171. Bidar's Cultural Legacy

  • Bidar became famous for:
  • Fort.
  • Madrasa.
  • Tombs.
  • Bidriware.
  • Persian-influenced court culture.

172. Gulbarga's Cultural Legacy

  • Gulbarga is especially associated with:
  • Early Bahmani capital.
  • Jama Masjid.
  • Haft Gumbaz.
  • Gesu Daraz.

173. Major Source Types

  • Knowledge of Bahmani history comes from:
  • Persian chronicles.
  • Inscriptions.
  • Coins.
  • Architecture.
  • Foreign accounts.
  • Regional literary traditions.

174. Firishta

  • Muhammad Qasim Firishta was a later Persian historian of the Deccan.
  • His historical work is an important source for medieval Deccan dynasties.
  • He lived mainly during the Bijapur Adil Shahi period, not the early Bahmani period itself.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Firishta → Later Deccan Historian, Not Contemporary with Bahmani Foundation

175. Burhan-i-Maasir

  • Burhan-i-Maasir by Sayyid Ali Tabataba is an important Persian historical source for the Bahmani and Deccan Sultanate world.

176. Numismatic Evidence

  • Bahmani coins help identify:
  • Royal titles.
  • Religious formulas.
  • Mint centres.
  • Political chronology.

177. Coinage

  • Bahmani rulers issued coins in:
  • Gold.
  • Silver.
  • Copper.
  • Monetary patterns were influenced by earlier Delhi and wider Islamic traditions.

178. Royal Titles

  • Bahmani rulers adopted Islamic royal titles including:
  • Shah.
  • Sultan.
  • Various honorific regnal titles.

179. Dynastic Name — Bahmani

  • The name "Bahmani" derives from the royal title Bahman Shah adopted by Hasan.
  • Claims connecting the dynasty to ancient Persian royal ancestry formed part of political legend and prestige.

180. TNPSC High-Yield Chronology

  • 1336 → Vijayanagara founded.
  • 1347 → Bahmani Kingdom founded.
  • 1347–1358 → Hasan Bahman Shah.
  • 1358–1375 → Muhammad Shah I.
  • 1397–1422 → Firuz Shah Bahmani.
  • 1422 → Ahmad Shah I.
  • 15th century → Capital shifted to Bidar.
  • 1481 → Mahmud Gawan executed.
  • c. 1490 onward → Major successor Sultanates emerge.
  • 1565 → Talikota fought by successor Sultanates against Vijayanagara.
  • 1686 → Bijapur annexed by Mughals.
  • 1687 → Golconda annexed by Mughals.

181. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings

  • Hasan Bahman Shah → Founder.
  • Gulbarga → First capital.
  • Bidar → Later capital.
  • Ahmad Shah Wali → Shift to Bidar.
  • Raichur Doab → Krishna–Tungabhadra.
  • Mahmud Gawan → Great minister.
  • Mahmud Gawan → Eight Tarafs.
  • Mahmud Gawan → Madrasa at Bidar.
  • Mahmud Gawan → Executed 1481.
  • Gesu Daraz → Gulbarga.
  • Bidriware → Bidar.
  • Ahmadnagar → Nizam Shahi.
  • Bijapur → Adil Shahi.
  • Berar → Imad Shahi.
  • Bidar → Barid Shahi.
  • Golconda → Qutb Shahi.

182. TNPSC Traps

  • Bahmani Kingdom was founded in 1347, not 1336.
  • Vijayanagara was founded in 1336.
  • Bahmani founder was Hasan Bahman Shah.
  • Gulbarga was the first capital.
  • Bidar became the later capital.
  • Raichur Doab lies between Krishna and Tungabhadra.
  • Bahmani–Vijayanagara rivalry was not purely religious; strategic and economic issues were fundamental.
  • Taraf means province.
  • Tarafdar means provincial governor.
  • Mahmud Gawan was a minister, not a Sultan.
  • Mahmud Gawan belonged to the Afaqi faction.
  • Deccani and Afaqi rivalry weakened the kingdom.
  • Mahmud Gawan divided the kingdom into eight Tarafs.
  • His madrasa is at Bidar.
  • He was executed in 1481.
  • His execution accelerated Bahmani decline.
  • The Bahmani Kingdom broke into five Deccan Sultanates.
  • Talikota was fought by Bahmani successor Sultanates, not the original unified Bahmani Kingdom.
  • Bidriware is associated with Bidar.
  • Gesu Daraz is associated with Gulbarga.
  • Firishta was a later Deccan historian.

183. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Vijayanagara → 1336.
  • Bahmani → 1347.
  • Founder → Hasan Bahman Shah.
  • First capital → Gulbarga.
  • Second capital → Bidar.
  • Ahmad Shah Wali → Bidar.
  • Raichur → Krishna + Tungabhadra.
  • Taraf → Province.
  • Tarafdar → Governor.
  • Gawan → Persian.
  • Gawan → Afaqi.
  • Gawan → 8 Tarafs.
  • Gawan → Land measurement.
  • Gawan → Bidar Madrasa.
  • Gawan → 1481.
  • Deccani vs Afaqi → Faction.
  • Gesu Daraz → Gulbarga.
  • Bidri → Bidar.
  • Nizam → Ahmadnagar.
  • Adil → Bijapur.
  • Imad → Berar.
  • Barid → Bidar.
  • Qutb → Golconda.
  • Talikota → 1565.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • When was the Bahmani Kingdom founded? → 1347 CE.
  • Who founded it? → Ala-ud-Din Hasan Bahman Shah.
  • What other name is associated with the founder? → Hasan Gangu.
  • During whose Delhi Sultanate reign did the Bahmani revolt occur? → Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
  • What did Bahmani independence indicate? → Collapse of effective Delhi control over much of the Deccan.
  • What was the first Bahmani capital? → Gulbarga.
  • What was Gulbarga also called under the Bahmanis? → Ahsanabad.
  • What was the later Bahmani capital? → Bidar.
  • Who shifted the capital to Bidar? → Ahmad Shah I Wali.
  • Which was Bahmani's major southern rival? → Vijayanagara Empire.
  • Which region was repeatedly contested? → Raichur Doab.
  • Raichur Doab lies between which rivers? → Krishna and Tungabhadra.
  • Name two important forts in the contested region. → Raichur and Mudgal.
  • Who succeeded Hasan Bahman Shah? → Muhammad Shah I.
  • Which ruler is an important late-fourteenth/early-fifteenth-century Bahmani scholar-king? → Firuz Shah Bahmani.
  • Firuz Shah's reign? → 1397–1422.
  • Who succeeded Firuz Shah? → Ahmad Shah I.
  • Another name of Ahmad Shah I? → Ahmad Shah Wali.
  • Where are Ahmad Shah Wali's tomb and shrine associated? → Ashtur near Bidar.
  • Who was the greatest Bahmani minister? → Mahmud Gawan.
  • Mahmud Gawan came from? → Persia.
  • Was Mahmud Gawan a Sultan? → No, he was the leading minister/Wazir.
  • Which Sultan's reign is especially associated with Mahmud Gawan? → Muhammad Shah III.
  • Who were the Afaqis? → Foreign-born or overseas-origin nobles.
  • Who were the Deccanis? → Older-established Muslim elites of the Deccan.
  • What major internal rivalry weakened the Bahmani Kingdom? → Deccani–Afaqi rivalry.
  • Which faction did Mahmud Gawan belong to? → Afaqi.
  • How many Tarafs were created under Mahmud Gawan's reorganisation? → Eight.
  • What was a Taraf? → Province.
  • Who administered it? → Tarafdar.
  • Why did Gawan reorganise provinces? → To reduce the power of provincial governors and strengthen the centre.
  • What revenue reform is associated with Gawan? → Measurement of land and more systematic revenue assessment.
  • What happened to important forts under his reforms? → Central control over them was strengthened.
  • Which educational institution did Mahmud Gawan build? → Mahmud Gawan Madrasa.
  • Where? → Bidar.
  • What architectural influence is visible in the Madrasa? → Persian influence.
  • When was Mahmud Gawan executed? → 1481.
  • Why was he executed? → Court rivals used a forged letter to accuse him of treason.
  • What was the effect of his execution? → It accelerated political decline.
  • What were the main causes of Bahmani decline? → Noble factionalism, weak rulers, provincial autonomy, succession struggles and Gawan's execution.
  • How many successor Sultanates emerged? → Five.
  • Name them. → Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Berar, Bidar and Golconda.
  • Ahmadnagar dynasty? → Nizam Shahi.
  • Founder associated with Ahmadnagar? → Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah.
  • Bijapur dynasty? → Adil Shahi.
  • Founder associated with Bijapur independence? → Yusuf Adil Shah.
  • Berar dynasty? → Imad Shahi.
  • Bidar dynasty? → Barid Shahi.
  • Golconda dynasty? → Qutb Shahi.
  • Who established the Qutb Shahi state? → Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk.
  • Did the unified Bahmani Kingdom fight at Talikota in 1565? → No.
  • Who fought Vijayanagara at Talikota? → Bahmani successor Sultanates.
  • Which four are principally associated with the Talikota coalition? → Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda and Bidar.
  • What was the main court language of the Bahmanis? → Persian.
  • Which regional language developed in the Deccan Muslim cultural environment? → Dakhni/Deccani.
  • Which important Sufi saint is associated with Gulbarga? → Khwaja Bande Nawaz Gesu Daraz.
  • Which Sufi order was Gesu Daraz associated with? → Chishti.
  • Which famous mosque is associated with Gulbarga? → Gulbarga Jama Masjid.
  • What is Haft Gumbaz? → Group of Bahmani royal tombs at Gulbarga.
  • Where are the later Bahmani royal tombs located? → Ashtur near Bidar.
  • Which famous metal craft developed at Bidar? → Bidriware.
  • What is Bidriware? → Silver inlay on a dark metal surface.
  • Why were western coastal ports important to Bahmani rulers? → Horse imports, maritime trade and customs revenue.
  • Which animal was especially important for imported military supply? → Horse.
  • What was the base of the Bahmani economy? → Agriculture.
  • Which crop benefited from Deccan black soil? → Cotton.
  • What is the Tamil Nadu relevance of Bahmani history? → Bahmani successor Sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota, weakening Vijayanagara control and contributing to greater autonomy of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee Nayaks.
  • Which later Sultanate had an important connection with the rise of Maratha families? → Ahmadnagar Nizam Shahi.
  • Which later Sultanates were annexed by Aurangzeb? → Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687.
  • Which empire was founded first: Vijayanagara or Bahmani? → Vijayanagara.
  • By how many years? → Eleven years.
  • What is the most important Bahmani administrative term for TNPSC? → Taraf.
  • What is the most important Bahmani minister for TNPSC? → Mahmud Gawan.
  • What is the most important Bahmani architectural-educational monument? → Mahmud Gawan Madrasa at Bidar.
  • What is the most important Bahmani internal political conflict? → Deccani versus Afaqi nobles.
  • What is the most important territorial dispute with Vijayanagara? → Raichur Doab.
